newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Albright says economy key to N. Korean peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Albright says economy key to N. Korean peace moves.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, visiting this heavily fortified outpost on an unstable border, said on Saturday the success of Korean peace talks depended heavily on how desparate Pyongyang was economically.
"It's very hard to predict," she told an American soldier when asked if South Korea and North Korea would finally negotiate a permanent end to their 1950-53 war.
"It basically depends on how much the North Koreans are hurting and whether they are willing to realise that a peaceful solution to this division is the way to go," she said.

Earlier in Seoul, 45 kms (30 miles) south of Panmunjon, Albright and South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha confirmed that preliminary peace talks with North Korea would be held on March 5 in New York.

At a news conference, they also reaffirmed support for the 1994 accord under which Washington, aided by Seoul and Tokyo, would provide $5 billion in light-water nuclear reactors to North Korea in return for Pyongyang freezing its nuclear programme.

Seoul's willingness to follow through on the pact often has been thrown in doubt, most recently when Pyongyang made threats, since toned down, about the defection of a high-level North Korean official to the South Korean Embassy in Beijing.

Albright conceded "frustrations" in dealing with the Stalinist North but stressed the "need to keep the implementation of the (1994) agreement on schedule, including light-water reactor construction."

Yoo held firm, however, on wide-scale food aid, which experts say must come largely from Seoul, in combination with commercial purchases, if North Korea's massive needs are to be served. "The issue of North Korea's food shortage is one of the important issues that we are dealing," he said.

But he cautioned that Pyongyang could only expect broad-scale aid after it engaged in peace talks, saying: "Once they come to the four-party talks, then we can also discuss the reduction of tension and building mutual confidence as well as the issue of the North Korean food shortage and this is all open."

The U.S. and South Korean presidents proposed the peace talks last year as a way to calm tensions on the peninsula and negotiate a peace treaty that would replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. China would be the other party.

North Korea twice before cancelled a "briefing" on the proposal in what was seen as an effort to press Washington to provide more food aid. U.S. officials said growing economic concerns make it likely Pyongyang will turn up on March 5.
The World Food Programme has estimated North Korea needs 2.3 million tons of grain this year to compensate for poor harvest and the effects of devastating 1995 and 1996 floods.
But it appealed recently only for $41.5 million -- equal to 100,000 tons -- because that was all the U.N. agency felt it could raise from South Korea and other key states at this time.
Beside the food problem, North Korea's economy has been deteriorating rapidly in recent years.
Yoo called North Korea "volatile" and said he agreed with Albright that "we have to avoid any clashes, armed clashes, between the two sides."

Like many U.S. leaders before her, Albright and her entourage helicoptered from Seoul to the demilitarised zone to meet some of the 1,200 American and South Korean soldiers at Outpost Ouellette, where she peered through high-powered binoculars to watch North Korean troops watching her.
Albright, wearing a personalised cap from the military unit, also had coffee with some of the soldiers, engaging them in conversation as easily as she had foreign ministers.

"When I was very young, I lived through the war in England and when I heard that the Yanks were coming that was the first time that I fell in love with American men in uniform," she said, praising their key role in U.S. national security.
